course.title: Blood Culture Sampling
course.splitRationale: The source names its own two sections and the split holds: slides 4-16 are 'what a blood culture is and what a good one requires', slides 17-39 are 'how you actually take one and what you are accountable for'. That is a shift from knowing to doing, and each half runs about 12 minutes of narration - comfortably inside one sitting. Each section ships as its own SCORM package with its own welcome, objectives and results slide, as this studio does.
course.learningTimeNote: Indicative seat time to work through the module once, attentively: narration at 140 words per minute, plus 6s per panel the learner opens, plus per-question time for each knowledge check, plus a 10% allowance for pauses, replays and navigation. On-screen text is not counted separately because it is revealed in step with the narration that explains it.

smeQueries.issue: The recommended adult blood volume is given two different ways. Slide 12 states 8-10 mL per bottle. Slide 22 states 20-30 mL per set, typically 10 mL in each bottle - which implies either a third bottle or 10-15 mL per bottle. The storyboard teaches 8-10 mL per bottle throughout, from slide 12. Please confirm the figure to teach, as this is the single most important determinant of culture yield and learners will be audited against it.
A text box reading 'Abnormal muscle function' appears on nine slides. Treated as leftover text from the deck this template was cloned from, and excluded. Please confirm it is not intended content.

The course menu and the Section 1 contents slide both list 'Common Bloodstream Pathogens' as a Section 1 topic, but the organisms slide sits at slide 31, inside Section 2. The storyboard places it at the end of Section 1, following the menu. Please confirm.

'Before starting antibiotics' appears in the indications list on slide 8, but it is a timing rule rather than an indication - the same point is made properly on slide 9. It has been kept in both places. Please confirm, or let us drop it from the indications list.

Two text problems in the source: the heading on slide 20 reads 'Proecdure', and the body placeholder on slide 16 repeats 'Order of Draw' twice. Both corrected silently. Flagging in case either signals missing content.

Slide 14 lists chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine and isopropyl alcohol as options with chlorhexidine preferred in adults; slide 21 instructs chlorhexidine specifically. Please confirm whether the procedure mandates chlorhexidine or allows the alternatives, and whether there is a paediatric or neonatal exception.
The CLSI blood culture guideline is cited as the 2007 approved guideline. Please confirm this is the edition in force at your institution, or supply the current one.

modules.scopingSentence: This module is divided into 2 sections. In this section, you will learn what a bloodstream infection is, what a blood culture does, and what a good specimen requires - timing, sets, volume, site, antisepsis and order of draw.

Identify the common causative organisms of bloodstream infection

props.text: This module is divided into 2 sections. In this section, you will learn what a bloodstream infection is, what a blood culture does, and what a good specimen requires - timing, sets, volume, site, antisepsis and order of draw.

slides.title: What this course covers
slides.designRationale: The source menu lists seventeen sub-topics, which is a table of contents rather than a screen. Collapsed to the eight topics of this section, with Section 2's eight reachable from its own menu - a learner choosing a topic should see choices, not an index.
slides.devNotes: Menu - each chip is a hotspot to that topic, with a visited state. Section 2 carries its own menu of the remaining eight topics.

interaction.note: Menu - each chip is a hotspot to that topic, with a visited state. Section 2 carries its own menu of the remaining eight topics.

slides.title: What is a bloodstream infection?
slides.designRationale: One idea stated precisely, with the clinical stakes beside it. A definition slide rather than bullets, because the whole module rests on understanding why a sterile compartment growing organisms is an emergency.

terms.description: Bacteria or fungi present in blood that is normally sterile
Can lead to sepsis  ·  may progress to septic shock  ·  requires rapid diagnosis and targeted antimicrobial therapy

props.alt: Clinician reviewing a deteriorating patient at the bedside, monitor visible

props.text: Untreated sepsis can progress to septic shock, multi-organ failure and death. Early identification through blood culture is what makes targeted therapy possible.

slides.title: What is a blood culture?
slides.designRationale: The second half of the definition pair, kept separate because the learner needs to hold 'what is wrong with the patient' and 'what the test does' as two distinct ideas before the procedure begins.

terms.description: A microbiological culture of peripheral blood - growth indicates systemic infection such as septicaemia

terms.term: What a positive culture gives you
terms.description: The causative organism identified, and antibiotic sensitivity tested

props.alt: Microbiology laboratory technician handling culture bottles in an incubator

slides.title: Collection has four steps
slides.designRationale: The source states these four steps in a sentence inside a paragraph, where they read as an aside. They are the spine of the whole module, so they get a numbered track of their own - the learner should be able to name them before meeting the nineteen detailed steps in Section 2.

slides.title: When to collect a blood culture
slides.designRationale: Nine indications, flat, no order, each short - icons so the eye lands on one at a time and the learner can recognise their own patient. A table has nothing to put in a second column.

props.text: When to collect a blood culture

slides.title: When to draw, and when not to wait
slides.designRationale: Four timing rules that each need a sentence of reasoning - 'obtain at onset of fever' means nothing without 'because that is when organisms are in the blood'. Chips with bodies, and the one rule that overrides the others pulled into a warning.

props.text: When to draw, and when not to wait

cards.title: Before the first dose of antibiotics
cards.body: Antibiotics reduce the chance of detecting the causative organism.

cards.title: At the onset of fever or chills
cards.body: Microorganisms are most likely to be present in the bloodstream at that moment.

cards.title: Immediately, if sepsis is suspected
cards.body: Do not wait for a fever spike and do not delay treatment.

cards.title: Multiple sets, separate sites
cards.body: Improves accuracy and helps distinguish true infection from contamination.

props.text: If sepsis is suspected, collect now. Never delay antibiotics waiting for a fever - treatment and collection happen together.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: A scenario rather than a recall question, placed immediately after the timing rules, because the judgement a nurse actually makes is whether a dose already given changes what they do.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: A patient with suspected bloodstream infection has already received one dose of antibiotics at another hospital. Which statement is most appropriate regarding blood culture collection?

options.text: Blood culture should not be collected
Blood culture should still be collected as soon as possible
Wait for 24 hours before collecting the sample
Collect only if the patient develops chills

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Although blood cultures are ideally collected before antibiotics, they should still be obtained if treatment has already started, as they may still identify the causative organism.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Although blood cultures are ideally collected before antibiotics, they should still be obtained if treatment has already started, as they may still identify the causative organism.

props.onSubmitWithNoSelection: show InvalidPrompt — do not fail silently

slides.title: How many sets?
slides.designRationale: Clinical situation against recommended sets - two-dimensional, so the source table is kept as a real table. A 'why' column surfaces the reasoning that was only in the narration, which is what turns a lookup into teaching.

rows: Improves detection of the causative organism
Accurate diagnosis and monitoring over time

props.text: Sets come from separate venipuncture sites. Two bottles drawn from one site is one set, not two.

slides.title: How much blood?
slides.designRationale: Age group against volume - a lookup the learner will return to, so a real table. This is the single highest-yield fact in the module, which is why it gets its own slide and a warning rather than a line inside the procedure.

props.text: Adequate blood volume is the single most important factor affecting culture yield. Under-filling a bottle is the commonest reason a real infection is missed.

slides.title: The blood culture set
slides.designRationale: A nurse has to recognise the two bottles on sight, find the volume markings and check the seal before they draw. That is learned by looking, not by reading, so it gets its own image-focus slide with the four things to check beside it.

items: Aerobic bottle - usually blue-capped, for organisms that need oxygen
Anaerobic bottle - usually purple or orange-capped, for organisms that do not
Volume markings on the label - fill to the mark, not by eye
Expiry date and an intact seal - check both before you start

props.alt: Pair of aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles side by side, labels and fill markings legible
props.searchTerms: aerobic anaerobic blood culture bottles pair

candidates.note: Bottle pairs - choose one where the fill markings and cap colours are clearly visible

props.text: Never use a bottle that is expired, leaking, or whose seal is broken. It will not support growth and the specimen will be rejected.

slides.title: Where to draw from
slides.designRationale: Three rules about site, each carrying a condition - 'avoid IV lines' is wrong without 'unless catheter infection is suspected'. Chips with bodies so the exception travels with the rule rather than being lost.

cards.title: Peripheral venipuncture is preferred
cards.body: Lower contamination risk and more reliable results

cards.title: Avoid drawing from intravenous lines
cards.body: Unless a catheter-related bloodstream infection is suspected

cards.title: Suspected central line infection
cards.body: One set from the catheter and one from a peripheral vein, for comparison

props.text: The paired draw is the point: if the catheter sample turns positive well before the peripheral one, the line is the source.

slides.title: Skin antisepsis
slides.designRationale: Antisepsis is a technique, not a fact - the motion, the coverage and the drying are all things the learner has to see performed. Its own image-focus slide, with the agents listed beside the image and the one rule that is most often broken as a warning.

items: Clean back-and-forth or in a circular motion, then let it dry

props.alt: Gloved hand cleaning a forearm venipuncture site with an antiseptic swab

candidates.note: Skin prep photos - choose one showing the swab in contact with the site

props.text: Let the antiseptic dry completely, and do not touch the site afterwards. Wet antiseptic has not worked yet, and a re-palpated site is contaminated.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: Added. Antisepsis and site selection were taught but never checked, and the drying rule is the single most broken step in the whole procedure - every distractor here is a real shortcut.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: You have cleaned the venipuncture site with chlorhexidine. The patient is restless and you are short of time. What should you do next?

options.text: Wipe the site dry with sterile gauze and proceed
Allow the antiseptic to dry completely, then proceed without touching the site
Re-palpate the vein to be certain, then proceed
Proceed immediately - chlorhexidine acts on contact

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Antiseptics need their full contact time to work, so the site must be allowed to air-dry completely. Wiping or re-palpating recontaminates a site that has already been cleaned.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Antiseptics need their full contact time to work, so the site must be allowed to air-dry completely. Wiping or re-palpating recontaminates a site that has already been cleaned.

slides.title: Order of draw depends on your device
slides.breadcrumb: Blood Culture Sampling / Order of draw
slides.designRationale: Two methods, opposite orders, and the reason is a single physical fact about air in the tubing. A comparison puts them side by side so the learner encodes the contrast rather than memorising one list and forgetting which it was.

props.text: Order of draw depends on your device

columns.title: Using a butterfly set
columns.body:
1. Aerobic bottle first
2. Anaerobic bottle second

Air in the tubing enters the first bottle - so it goes to the one that tolerates air

columns.title: Using a syringe
columns.body:
1. Anaerobic bottle first
2. Aerobic bottle second

No air in the line - so the anaerobic bottle is protected by filling first

props.text: Remember it by the air: with tubing, the air has somewhere to go first - aerobic. With a syringe there is none, so protect the anaerobic bottle first.

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: Placed after sets, volume and order of draw, where the learner has met all three reasons multiple sets exist and can discriminate the real one from three plausible but wrong purposes.

props.text: Select the correct answer and click Submit.

props.stem: Which of the following is the primary purpose of collecting multiple blood culture sets?

options.text: To improve pathogen detection and differentiate contamination from true infection

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: Multiple sets increase diagnostic sensitivity and help distinguish true bacteraemia from contaminated samples.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: Multiple sets increase diagnostic sensitivity and help distinguish true bacteraemia from contaminated samples.

props.onSubmitWithNoSelection: show InvalidPrompt — do not fail silently

slides.title: Check your understanding!
slides.designRationale: Added. The learner's real task is performing a sequence under time pressure, so the check asks them to sequence it. A multiple-choice version would test which list they memorised rather than whether they can run it.

props.text: You are drawing with a butterfly set. Drag the steps into the order you perform them, then click Submit.

items.label: Clean the skin and let the antiseptic dry completely
Invert both bottles gently to mix

feedback.heading: That's incorrect!
feedback.body: With a butterfly set the aerobic bottle is filled first, because air in the tubing enters the first bottle. With a syringe the order reverses. Mixing comes last, once both bottles are filled.

feedback.heading: That's correct!
feedback.body: With a butterfly set the aerobic bottle is filled first, because air in the tubing enters the first bottle. With a syringe the order reverses. Mixing comes last, once both bottles are filled.

slides.title: Common bloodstream pathogens
slides.designRationale: Three named groups, each with its own organisms - chips with bodies, because the group is what the learner should retain and the organisms support it. Grouping by Gram stain and fungi is also how the laboratory will report back.

cards.title: Gram-positive
cards.body: Staphylococcus aureus  ·  Coagulase-negative staphylococci  ·  Streptococci  ·  Enterococci

props.text: Coagulase-negative staphylococci appear in both lists in this module - as a true pathogen here, and as the commonest contaminant in Section 2. The difference is how many bottles grew it.
